citations.clause: Storage requirements and retention controls per endpoint, /v1/audio/transcriptions row
citations.quote: /v1/audio/transcriptions | Data used for training: No | Abuse monitoring retention: None | Application state retention: None | Zero Data Retention eligible: Yes

By default, abuse monitoring logs are generated for all API feature usage and retained for up to 30 days, unless longer retention is required by law, or is reasonably necessary to protect our services or any third party from harm.
Currently, these controls are subject to prior approval by OpenAI and acceptance of additional requirements.

dispositions.ownerDecision: Owner decision, not provider evidence: OpenAI is the pinned transcription provider and the default API data policy is the selected retention control. Zero Data Retention is not requested and not active, so it must not be recorded as the ceiling even though this endpoint is listed as eligible. Activating ZDR needs an OpenAI org-level approval and is an owner action outside this contract. The endpoint table's None is OpenAI's published figure, not something SnapList has observed, so the row keeps provider-owned treatment and does not promise the seller that no copy exists. This row is pinned to one adapter on purpose: ADR-0011 keeps seller voice context provider-neutral and docs/contracts/voice-context-v1.json does not freeze the provider or model, so activating a non-OpenAI transcription adapter reopens this row and its retention must be re-cited before that adapter carries seller audio.

Deleting it at consumption would make the exception unauditable and let the same account be granted a second one.

dispositions.ownerDecision: Issue #524 accepts that the fence's durability depends on an Apple-owned bit SnapList cannot erase. This is the deliberate trade for blocking unmetered provider spend, and the seller-facing appeal path is the audited one-time support override rather than a bit reset.

citations.clause: Section 9 (Protecting User Privacy), Collecting and Storing Personal Information
citations.quote: You agree to promptly delete Personal Information on the earlier of: (i) when required by your data privacy and data retention policies; (ii) when requested by eBay or by the applicable eBay User to whom the Personal Information pertains, (iii) when the Personal Information is no longer necessary for the specific, legitimate purpose for which it was collected or processed for your Application, or (iv) when your participation in the Program is terminated.

You must destroy all copies of, or anything containing, eBay Content and Personal Information in your possession within ten (10) days after termination, and you will provide written certification of destruction to eBay upon eBay’s request.

dispositions.ownerDecision: Owner decision, not provider evidence: eBay-issued offer and listing identifiers stored against a seller are classified as Personal Information under the Section 1 definition, because they are received from eBay through the Program and indirectly identify an eBay User. eBay has not been asked to confirm this and the conservative reading is deliberate. If eBay later states these identifiers are not Personal Information, the only cost of this choice is a deleted column nobody was reading.

dispositions.maximumRetention: for the account lifetime; account erasure deletes the Clerk user and verifies its absence in the same operation. Clerk's public documentation states no post-deletion backup or archive window, so SnapList claims none
dispositions.completionProof: after clerkClient.users.deleteUser(userId), reading that user back through the Clerk Backend API reports it absent with status 404. A user.deleted webhook is an acknowledgement that the request was accepted and is never accepted as proof on its own. The executable form of this proof is src/lib/retention-contract/clerk-identity-absence.test.ts. OBSERVED 2026-07-26 against a live Clerk development instance (sk_test_ secret, no production data): the suite created a user, read it back successfully by id, called deleteUser on it, and the subsequent read of the same id was reported absent — status 404, error code resource_not_found, longMessage 'No user was found with id <deleted id>'. The test asserts the reported 404 status rather than merely that the read rejected, so a network or auth failure cannot be mistaken for absence. It skips when no sk_test_ CLERK_RETENTION_PROOF_SECRET_KEY is configured, so CI, which runs without secrets, does not re-observe this proof

citations.quote: We store the personal information we collect as described in this Privacy Policy for as long as you use our Services or as necessary to fulfill the purpose(s) for which it was collected, provide our Services, resolve disputes, establish legal defenses, conduct audits, pursue legitimate business purposes, enforce our agreements, and comply with applicable laws.

dispositions.ownerDecision: Owner decision, not provider evidence: the verified-absence branch is selected instead of waiting on Clerk to describe its internal backup retention. Clerk's published retention clause is duration-by-purpose and states no numeric window, so a cited maximum is not available from the provider. Observed absence through Clerk's own API is what SnapList proves and all it claims. That proof has now been performed rather than merely defined: the absence test was run once against a Clerk development instance on 2026-07-26 and the observed result is recorded in completionProof. The same accepted-versus-verified distinction that blocked this row was applied to the proof itself, which is why the row waited for an observed run instead of asserting that the test would pass.

For In-App Purchases made using alternative payment processing or linking out to a webpage, you're responsible for taxes, including (but not limited to):
A UUID you create at the time of purchase that associates the transaction with a customer on your own service.
Deleting customers through the RevenueCat dashboard or API clears out all of their data and is sufficient for GDPR erasure requests.
Deleting a customer will also remove all their purchase history for sandbox and production data

dispositions.ownerDecision: Owner decision, not provider evidence, on three points. Apple charges the customer for the transaction including any applicable taxes, never discloses the customer to the developer, and keeps the payout and financial reports in App Store Connect that are the tax record. For customers of Apple Distribution International Ltd. or Apple Services Pte. Ltd. the cited terms name that entity the merchant of record; elsewhere the terms make the transaction a contract with Apple. The conclusion rests on who charges the customer and who holds the records, which holds either way. First, SnapList's Apple and RevenueCat references are an entitlement mapping, not a tax record: the stored rows carry a Clerk user id, a RevenueCat app user id, an Apple original transaction id, and allowance state, and carry no customer identity, price, or tax amount. Apple never discloses the customer to the developer; the only per-customer link is a UUID the developer itself creates. So the row is deleted at account erasure rather than retained for a fixed number of years, and the 7-year fallback is deliberately not used. This conclusion has not been reviewed by a tax professional. Second, one RevenueCat customer is the original_app_user_id plus its aliases array, so deleting the customer deletes the whole alias set; that follows from the two cited clauses read together rather than from a single sentence stating it. Third, RevenueCat's public documentation does not state that deletion is synchronous, so completion requires reading the customer back rather than trusting the delete response. If SnapList ever adopts alternative payment processing or external purchase links, Apple stops collecting the tax and this row must be reopened.

dispositions.maximumRetention: 30 days after the erasure reaches a completed status; the raw Clerk user id, RevenueCat app user ids, SnapList user id, and Idempotency-Key are removed at the moment a completed status is written, leaving only a one-way digest, the status, and any retained-record labels. An erasure that is still unfinished, including one parked in deletion_needs_attention, keeps those identifiers because resuming the deletion requires them, and is not pruned until it completes
dispositions.completionProof: the private prune result and durable absence prove no receipt older than the window remains; cron.job registration and cron.job_run_details prove at least one successful prune in every rolling 24 hours
dispositions.ownerDecision: The receipt is the one row account erasure deliberately does not delete with the account, so it is named here rather than left implicit. It exists because a durable erasure must answer a replayed Idempotency-Key with the generation it already resolved to, and must keep refusing writes to an account that is gone; both answers are impossible once the record itself is deleted. It is not tenant data and is not reachable by the tenant: it lives in `private`, is keyed by a SHA-256 digest of a fixed constant prefix and the user id rather than by the id, and is scrubbed of every raw identifier the instant a completed status is written, so what outlives the account cannot re-identify the person. The digest is deliberately not described as salted: the prefix is a domain separator carried in the migration source, not a secret, and what defeats enumeration is the entropy of a Clerk user id rather than anything withheld from an attacker who has the source. An erasure that has not completed still holds the raw identifiers, because resuming the deletion needs them; that is a bounded window on unfinished work rather than a retention decision, and the row is pruned only after it completes. The 30-day window is an owner judgement, not a provider requirement: long enough that a client retrying a stalled erasure still resolves to its own generation, short enough that the digest does not become indefinite retention. Issue #384 owns it.
